query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Using a combined experimental and computational approach—specifically, high-throughput differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), in-situ high-temperature diffraction, and CALPHAD-based thermodynamic simulations—will enable accurate and efficient determination of the melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a wide range of high-entropy alloys (HEAs).
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or homogenized multi-principal-element alloys prepared in an inert or vacuum environment, ensuring well-controlled composition and minimal contamination before measurement and modeling.
generation.intervention: Systematic compositional variation and sample preparation, followed by rapid DSC scans to measure thermal events, in-situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction to track volume changes, and thermodynamic assessments via advanced CALPHAD calculations.
generation.conditions: Measurements performed from room temperature up to and slightly above the melting range of each alloy under inert or vacuum atmosphere; thermodynamic modeling performed over the same temperature interval with HPC resources to systematically explore compositional and temperature-dependent behavior.
generation.structural_mediator: Real-time observation of lattice expansion and phase evolution (from solid to liquid) via high-temperature diffraction, complemented by computed Gibbs energies and phase equilibria from CALPHAD databases.
generation.mechanism: Integration of precise calorimetric signals (onset/peak of melting, enthalpy) with structural insights from diffraction and robust thermodynamic predictions allows direct and self-consistent derivations of fusion properties and volume changes while capturing the multicomponent interactions characteristic of high-entropy alloys.
generation.predicted_outcome: This integrated method will attain melting temperatures accurate to within ±10–20 K, enthalpy and entropy of fusion within ±5%, and volume-change data within ±1–2% for a broad spectrum of HEA compositions.
generation.baseline: Conventional single-sample DSC characterization and simplified mixing rules can yield significantly larger uncertainties, especially given the compositional complexity of HEAs, making a purely empirical or classical approach less reliable.
generation.boundary: The approach is best applied to metallic multi-principal-element alloys that crystallize in relatively simple structures. It may be less accurate for alloys with extensive chemical short-range order or highly complex stoichiometric intermetallic phases that are poorly captured by current CALPHAD databases.
generation.uncertainty: Potential inconsistencies may arise from incomplete thermodynamic databases for complex HEAs, instrumentation limits in scanning speed or temperature calibration, and unforeseen metastable phases not accounted for in the models.

falsification_experiment.design: Select representative HEAs spanning a wide compositional space and produce replicate samples. Carry out side-by-side measurements of melting temperature, enthalpy/entropy of fusion, and volume change on heating among three methods: the proposed combined DSC/diffraction/CALPHAD workflow, standard DSC alone, and direct thermal analysis via a well-established technique (e.g., drop calorimetry). Compare measured and predicted thermophysical properties from each.
measurements: Onset and peak melting temperatures from DSC and drop calorimetry
Total enthalpy and entropy of fusion from DSC
Temperature-dependent lattice parameters from in-situ X-ray diffraction
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If significant discrepancies appear among the integrated (DSC + diffraction + CALPHAD) measurements versus the independent control methods, or if the approach fails to reliably capture known reference materials’ melting and thermophysical properties to within the stated uncertainty ranges, the hypothesis would be invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: The paper studies new materials for brake disks used in car manufacturing. The materials used in the manufacturing of the brake disc must adapt and correlate with the challenges of current society. There is a tremendous interest in the development of a material that has high strength, good heat transfer, corrosion resistance and low density, in order to withstand high-breaking forces, high heat and various adverse environment. Low-density materials improve fuel efficiency and environmental impact. Complex concentrated alloys (CCA) are metallic element mixtures with multi-principal elements, which can respond promisingly to this challenge with their variety of properties. Several compositions were studied through thermodynamic criteria calculations (entropy of mixing, enthalpy of mixing, lambda coefficient, etc.) and CALPHAD modeling, in order to determine appropriate structures. The selected compositions were obtained in an induction furnace with a protective atmosphere and then subjected to an annealing process. AbstractThe ability to predict and understand phases in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) is still being debated, and primarily true predictive capabilities derive from the known thermodynamics of materials. The present work demonstrates that prior work using high-throughput first-principles calculations may be further utilized to provide direct insight into the temperature- and composition-dependent phase evolution in HEAs, particularly Al-containing HEAs with a strengthening multiphase microstructure. Using a simple model with parameters derived from first-principles calculations, we reproduce the major features associated with Al-containing phases, demonstrating a generalizable approach for exploring potential phase evolution where little experimental data exists. Neutron scattering, in situ microscopy, and calorimetry measurements suggest that our high-throughput Monte Carlo technique captures both qualitative and quantitative features for both intermetallic phase formation and microstructure evolution at lower temperatures. AbstractDeveloping affordable and light high-temperature materials alternative to Ni-base superalloys has significantly increased the efforts in designing advanced ferritic superalloys. However, currently developed ferritic superalloys still exhibit low high-temperature strengths, which limits their usage. Here we use a CALPHAD-based high-throughput computational method to design light, strong, and low-cost high-entropy alloys for elevated-temperature applications. Through the high-throughput screening, precipitation-strengthened lightweight high-entropy alloys are discovered from thousands of initial compositions, which exhibit enhanced strengths compared to other counterparts at room and elevated temperatures. The experimental and theoretical understanding of both successful and failed cases in their strengthening mechanisms and order-disorder transitions further improves the accuracy of the thermodynamic database of the discovered alloy system. This study shows that integrating high-throughput screening, multiscale modeling, and experimental validation proves to be efficient and useful in accelerating the discovery of advanced precipitation-strengthened structural materials tune

AbstractThe third-generation thermodynamic descriptions for Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems were performed to construct the reliable thermodynamic database for refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) containing Laves phase. The third-generation Gibbs energy expressions of pure Cr and V in both solid and liquid phases were established, from which the thermodynamic properties and thermal vacancy can be well described. The thermodynamic descriptions of Ta-Cr and Ta-V over the whole composition and temperature regions were carried out based on the reviewed phase equilibria and thermodynamic data with the CALPHAD (CALculation of PHAse Diagrams) approach. Specifically, the thermodynamic parameters of C14 and C15 Laves phases were evaluated by combining the theoretically computed and experimentally measured thermodynamic properties as well as the semiempirical relations. The calculated phase diagrams and thermodynamic properties in Ta-Cr and Ta-V systems according to the present thermodynamic parameters had a nice agreement with the experimental data even down to 0 K, indicating the reliability of the present modeling.Keywords: third-generation thermodynamic description, Ta-Cr system, Ta-V s
